item.title: Connect DeepSeek V4 to Codex: Solving API Format Incompatibility with a Proxy Script
item.description:
🚀 Proxy script is now open source: Siborne/any2codex — one-click conversion of any third-party API to Codex-compatible format. Not just DeepSeek.

Where Does the Problem Come From?

DeepSeek V4 series models recently went on sale, offering exceptional value. Many developers want to switch to them within Codex. But in practice, they run into a frustrating issue:

Codex’s API request format doesn’t match the DeepSeek official API.

Specifically, Codex internally sends requests in a fixed path format. If you simply change the endpoint to DeepSeek’s official https://api.deepseek.com in the config, Codex will error out — no matter how you tweak the model name or parameters, nothing works.

Why Do Proxy Services Work?

This actually hints at the solution. The reason third-party API proxy services can seamlessly integrate with Codex is that they perform a layer of protocol adaptation — intercepting Codex’s requests, reassembling them into the format the target API expects, forwarding them, and then translating the response back into a format Codex understands.

With this in mind, we can apply the exact same approach: build our own local proxy script to bridge Codex and the DeepSeek API.

Architecture Overview

The overall flow looks like this:

Codex Client
    │
    ▼
CC Switch (model configuration layer)
    │
    ▼
Local Proxy Script (protocol conversion layer)
    │
    ▼
DeepSeek Official API

Three components, each with a clear role:

Component Responsibility
CC Switch Open-source model switcher; injects custom model configs into Codex
Proxy Script Local proxy service; bidirectional request/response format conversion
DeepSeek API The actual model service handling user requests

Step-by-Step Guide

Step 1: Prepare the Tools

  • CC Switch: Open-source tool, available on the Microsoft Store or GitHub
  • Codex: Your IDE, already in use
  • Proxy Script: Siborne/any2codex, one-click conversion of third-party APIs to Codex-compatible format

Step 2: Configure CC Switch

Open CC Switch, find the Codex / OpenAI Codex configuration entry, and click the plus icon to create a custom config:

  • Endpoint: Set to your local proxy script address, e.g., http://localhost:<port>/v1
  • Model name: The DeepSeek model you want, e.g., deepseek-v4-pro or deepseek-v4-fast
  • API Key: Use a fixed placeholder (your real API key is embedded in the proxy script)

⚠️ Critical: The endpoint here must NOT be the official DeepSeek address. Codex sends requests in a fixed path format, and direct connection to the official API will fail due to format mismatch. Requests must go through the proxy script first.

Save the configuration.

Step 3: Start the Proxy Script

Run the script. It will first perform a connectivity check, verifying your API key is valid and the network is reachable. Once verified, it starts a local proxy service and begins listening for requests from Codex.

Step 4: Switch Models in Codex

Open Codex, find the custom configuration injected by CC Switch in the model selection list (it will appear with the name you set in Step 2), and select it.

Send a quick test message — if everything is working, DeepSeek V4’s response will appear right in front of you.

What Does the Proxy Script Actually Do?

The core logic is straightforward:

  1. Receive requests from Codex in the fixed format
  2. Parse out the effective fields: messages, model, parameters, etc.
  3. Reassemble them into the request body format required by the DeepSeek official API
  4. Forward to DeepSeek servers with your real API key
  5. Restore the response into Codex-compatible format and return it to the client

At its core, it’s a protocol conversion layer.

Why Can’t We Just Modify Codex’s Request Path?

The instinctive reaction is: “Can’t I just find where Codex defines the request path and change it to DeepSeek’s format?”

Turns out you really can’t. The video author mentioned trying many times — changing /chat, /v1, various path segments — Codex errors out every time. The request format is hardcoded in Codex’s internal logic, and tampering with it breaks the entire communication flow. Rather than fighting Codex’s internals, it’s far cleaner to add an adaptation layer on the outside.

Summary

Approach Direct endpoint change Proxy script
Does it work? ❌ Errors out ✅ Works
Implementation cost Low (one config line) Medium (run one extra script)
Maintainability Poor (breaks on Codex updates) Good (decoupled, no dependency on Codex internals)
Extensibility None High (easily add more models)

The insight here is quite generalizable — this isn’t just about using DeepSeek with Codex. Any scenario with similar API format incompatibility can be solved with a local proxy layer. CC Switch handles config injection, and the proxy script handles protocol conversion. Together, they open the door to connecting all kinds of third-party models to Codex.

The proxy script is open source at Siborne/any2codex. Stars and PRs welcome — let’s build out compatibility for more models together.

Source: Bilibili video Codex接入国产大模型教程 by 王了小王 (2026-05-06)
